title: Food insecurity/neurotic traits and dieting
summary: He argues there is no universal diet and that your psychology, culture, ancestry and childhood shape which diet approach works. People with food insecurity may suffer from keeping the pantry empty; anxiety around food should be minimized, and the ideal is an unemotional, 'professional' relationship with food, illustrated by his own mass obsession up to 240 lbs.

claims.claim: For him, training matters more than diet, and he is still learning what his body likes to eat.
There is no universal diet; you should understand your ancestry and listen to your body, since some foods that are technically good may not agree with you.
Your culture and personality type also affect how you consume food, and your relationship with food affects your body and diet.
If you grew up with food insecurity, the strategy of keeping no snacks at home to avoid cheating can create heavy psychological stress.

He feels excellent after grocery shopping and uneasy with an empty fridge despite having plenty of money, so restricting groceries doesn't work for him; instead he uses discipline, e.g. making a month's snacks last a month.
If you lack self-control when food is available, keeping little food at home may be the right route; the stress that having or not having food causes is a key indicator of which diet to follow.

If you can eat intuitively, roughly know your calorie needs and hit macros and micros without calculating, do that; he does, and has never had anxiety about meeting his training's nutritional requirements.
Pick some areas of life to be low-stress in because others will always be high-stress; for him diet is the low-stress area.
Counting macros or calories is not stupid; it is a means to an end, and if weighing everything makes you feel better, do it. Don't let anxiety grow until it stalls your gains.
Childhood status shapes eating: former fat kids may cling to comfort food or starve themselves; former skinny kids may overeat to compensate or stay stuck wanting to be skinny.
Fixing your relationship with food is vital and should be done as early as possible, through self-work or therapy if needed.
As a former skinny kid he became mass-obsessed, reaching 240 lbs; ankle pain, knee pain and broken ribs that wouldn't heal under the weight made him accept losing weight.
Many very underweight or overweight people are listening to their mind, not their body; the body signals hunger appropriately to maintain its mass, though appetite hormones make it more complex.
Keep your relationship with food 'professional', without emotional attachment, so you can see food as sustenance without psychological stress clouding your judgment.
Food is also culture and connection, and eating animals raises questions about how we justify absorbing another life; rituals around consuming animal products may be beneficial (future video).
He doesn't care about insulin/carbs/protein talk because he never had to; his diet content will stay somewhat spiritual.
